specialist_findings.claim: The `consistent-type-assertions` suppressions in test fakes (section 5) are addressed by 'narrow DI interfaces', but the plan does not specify what the narrow interface looks like or how the fake will satisfy it without assertions. For fakes that mirror complex SDK types (curriculum-sdk, stdio), the interface surface is non-trivial — an under-specified narrow interface risks either being too broad (still needing assertions) or too narrow (hiding real type mismatches between fake and production type). The plan should name the critical interface members or point to an existing DI interface pattern to validate the approach is tractable.

Section 7 (Miscellaneous) lists `no-explicit-any` among the rules to remediate and names 'narrow interfaces for type assertions' as the strategy, but also bundles `no-misused-promises` (requiring async wrappers) and `no-restricted-types` (WeakSet, thrown-value `object`) under the same single-sentence rationale. These are structurally distinct type problems: `no-explicit-any` needs genuine type modelling; `no-misused-promises` is a call-site async discipline issue; `no-restricted-types` requires either a type-safe wrapper or a library substitution. Conflating them under one execution item (`miscellaneous`) means no single fix strategy is validated before execution and creates a risk that one sub-category is blocked while another is not.

The logger strategy (section 4, line 99) proposes replacing custom sanitisation with `safe-stable-stringify`, asserting it 'absorbs' `WeakSet<object>` and thrown-value `object` types that trigger `no-restricted-types`. This is a type-level claim that is not verified in the plan — `safe-stable-stringify` is a runtime serialiser and its TypeScript typings may still expose `object` or `unknown` at the call boundary, leaving residual `no-restricted-types` violations. The plan should cite the library's declared input type or note that a thin typed wrapper will be needed.

The `typeSafeEntries`/`typeSafeKeys`/`typeSafeValues` helpers referenced in section 7 are named but not located. The plan cites `packages/core/oak-eslint/src/rules/no-eslint-disable.ts` as a reference but does not point to the type-helper utilities. If these are in `type-helpers/src/index.ts` (the user-approved exceptions file mentioned at line 179), there is a subtle risk: consuming those helpers from the same file listed as an exception boundary may accidentally pull suppression patterns into non-excepted code. The plan should confirm the helper source and that it is importable from the target files without crossing the exception boundary.

Generated data files (section 2) triggering `max-lines` contain TypeScript type literals (thread-progression-data.ts at 1,529 lines, ontology-data.ts at 582 lines). The JSON-loader strategy is correct for type safety — moving inline TS literals to JSON and pairing with a `types.ts` is the right approach. The plan already proved this pattern; no type-specific risk here beyond confirming the generated `types.ts` keeps the discriminated union or branded-type precision currently present in the inline TS literals.

specialist_findings.claim: WS2 triage rubric is well-formed and grounded in testing-strategy.md. The six disposition categories (useless→delete, pins-internals→reshape, provable-lower→push-down, re-proves-elsewhere→delete-higher, genuine-behaviour-proof→convert, test-narrowing-guard→assert-whole-value) are exhaustive and mutually exclusive. The falsifiability, raw-library, and assert-effects screens are correctly differentiated for unit vs integration scale.

Atomic-landing invariant is stated and enforced: when a test conversion requires a product-code change (throw→Result), both land in the same commit. This is the correct discipline and is correctly placed in WS2 acceptance.

WS2 acceptance says 'the touched workspace's lint+type-check+test gate is green' but applies only 'per batch' — there is no per-commit gate requirement stated. If batches span multiple commits, a red intermediate commit could slip through. The atomic-landing rule implies per-commit green is required; the acceptance language should make that explicit rather than leaving it to 'per batch'.

WS2 disposition log ('non-code proof for deletions') names the failed screen but does not specify a durable home for the log (unlike WS0's survey, which is explicitly homed to .agent/reports/agentic-engineering/). If the log is ephemeral or per-session, deletion rationales will be unrecoverable at WS4's reassessment gate.

The integration-test carve-out in the falsifiability screen ('integration tests differ: assert composed behaviour across wired units that cannot be proven at a lower level') is correct in principle but has no stated operationalisation test. Without a concrete check — e.g. 'does the test wire at least two real units without stubs for the path under test?' — a reviewer applying the screen cannot distinguish a legitimate integration test from a unit test with too many real dependencies. This risks either under-deletion (the screen is too permissive) or over-deletion (the reviewer applies the naive unit-scale screen to integration tests).

WS2 is PRIORITY and depends only on WS0 (line 19), but the text at line 153 states 'WS1 (fix-review) before WS2/WS3 — its minimum shippable shape is the four-conversion adversarial verdict; if a conversion is a hack, remediate before building more on the same pattern.' If ws1 reveals assertNeverResult is a hack (which blocks ws2/ws3 per line 154-157), the missing dependency edge means an executor reading only the front-matter would start WS2 on a hacked keystone. The blocking coupling is documented in prose but not enforced by the dependency structure.

WS3 acceptance requires 'streamable-http *.e2e.test.ts green' and the proof contract calls for e2e+integration+unit. This is the strongest proof tier in the plan and is appropriate given that template changes regenerate output consumed at runtime. No test-lens concern here.

The test-narrowing-guard category (a throw used only to enable TypeScript narrowing inside a test body) is described as 'remove the guard' and 'assert the whole value and keep the test'. There is no stated proof that removing the narrowing guard leaves the test still type-checking. If the guard feeds a narrowed type downstream in the test body, removing it without a type assertion or value-level restructure will produce a type error. The acceptance does not name type-check as a required gate for this specific category (it names lint+type-check+test only 'per batch', not per individual disposition).
